content:
Episode 5 SEC — Introduction: Argumentative Writing Genres

In this episode I will identify the essential standards-based skills that we are to teach within argumentative writing units.

Throughout our daily lives, we encounter differing viewpoints in a variety of situations. We learn what others think based on their social media posts and online blogs. We learn of people's beliefs by reading bumper stickers and editorial cartoons. And while we are all entitled to our own opinions, if we want to persuade someone to agree with us, to convince him that OUR position is the strongest, then our opinion requires support in the form of reasons and evidence.

This combination of opinion plus support is evident within a variety of genres. Commercials, advertisements, and political propaganda each make a claim and support it in order to convince others to buy or do something. A recommendation is a personal endorsement or testimonial based on reasons given by the writer about his own experience. Persuasive letters and speeches have a direct audience and thus provide very targeted reasons. While a persuasive essay, which reaches a broader audience, is more formal in tone and more universal in reasoning. Short constructed responses are a popular genre included within many state reading assessments. These require the student to draw a conclusion or make an inference and support it with evidence from the text.

All of these are one-sided arguments. They include the writer's claim and support for it.

Episode 5 SEC — Counterclaim Standards Progression Grades 6-12

As we move from elementary standards into middle school, a new ingredient is required within argumentative pieces — the reference to opposing viewpoints. We juggle multiple sides whenever we make a pro-con list or participate in a debate. And in the secondary classroom, we often see a transition from informative-research writing to argumentative. Students go beyond explaining problems and solutions or outlining causes and effects. Rather, they argue which is the BIGGEST problem, or SIMPLEST solution, or which cause or effect is MOST impactful.

At the high school level, the argument analysis also appears. While this task DOES generate an argumentative product, the student is not writing about a topic or issue. Rather, he's assessing the strengths and weaknesses of someone else's argument. More precisely, the writer demonstrates his knowledge of what a STRONG two-sided argument should include and evaluates a piece of writing for those facets.

Now state standards don't typically name WHICH genres of argumentative writing that you are to teach. Rather they more broadly state that you are to TEACH students HOW to write arguments. While they increase in rigor, there are 4 core ingredients of argumentative writing that are to be the focus of our whole class mini-lessons: 1. Introduce the claim and counterclaim. 2. Provide reasons. 3. Support with evidence. 4. Conclude the writing.

Episode 5 SEC — Counterclaim Expectations by Grade Level

It's clear that starting in grade 8 students should be addressing the opposition within their writing. But look at sixth grade — there is NOTHING highlighted, and that's because there is NO reference to the opposition. Although the sixth-grade standard begins with "Write arguments," this is simply a reference to the broader writing mode. There are many types or genres of argumentative writing, and the opening statement of this standard uses the word "argument" as a generic term, as an overview. The specific expectations are actually detailed below it, in that a, b, c list of grade level skills. In most states, the sixth-grade standards do not mention counterclaims. While you will want to verify this with your own state's standards, you'll likely find that most task sixth grade with teaching students to master the ONE-sided argument.

So if there's no mentioning of the opposition in the sixth grade standard, but it's there in grade 8, let's insert grade 7 to see what it states. Ok, so seventh graders have to "acknowledge the opposition." Let's compare that to eighth grade, where students must acknowledge the opposition AND address it within the body. OK, that's definitely a higher expectation. Let's continue looking up to grades 9-10 and 11-12. NOW the standards state that the opposition must be developed. Thus the counterclaim has to be introduced, explained, and supported with evidence. ADDITIONALLY a high-schooler has to show how HIS OWN claim has weaknesses and limitations.

The standards for grades 8-12 involve a significant increase in rigor and complexity regarding counterclaims. While sixth-grade teachers may feel tempted to provide instruction on the opposition, it's important to remember the crucial role that you play. Your students need to master writing one-sided arguments because the grade levels after you won't have time to teach these foundational skills.

Additionally, anyone working with writers who are still learning to put together sentences, like English language learners or those with special needs, you may find the ELEM version of this content more appropriate as it addresses these same 4 essential skills but at various developmental stages.

section_name: Skill 1 — Introduce the Claim: Debatable Topics
content:
Episode 5 SEC — Skill #1: Introduce the Claim and Counterclaim

The standards SIMPLY state students need to "introduce the claim." Consequently many teachers begin their instruction with HOW to write a claim. But that assumes students know what a claim is and that it's based on having made a decision about something that was debatable. If students come to you knowing this, great, but it's often necessary to do a little front loading first.

Start instruction by comparing the informative and argumentative icons. Point out that in the informative icon the writer is above the reader. He is telling or teaching the reader. But in the argumentative icon, the writer is level with the reader. He's talking to the reader. They end up shaking hands like they are on the same page. They are in agreement.

Similarly explain the difference between informative and argumentative TOPICS — and the key discerning factor is debatability. An argumentative topic finds controversy in a subject. For example, "athletes who experience concussions" is NOT an argumentative topic. It's an informative that will likely provide the causes and effects of concussions, and what it feels like to sustain one. We need students to understand that an argument is made about a FACET of the subject, a controversial component — like what should the school's policy be before returning to play after sustaining a concussion. Advocating for a particular outcome is the purpose of argumentative writing. This is especially important if students are choosing the topics they will write arguments about.

section_name: Skill 1 — Identify, List, Study, Decide Process
content:
Episode 5 SEC — Skill #1: Identify, List, Study, Decide — Choosing the Strongest Side

After clarifying that topics must be debatable, then it's important to quickly curb students' instincts to "pick a side." While everyone can have an opinion, the goal of an argumentative writer is to persuade the reader to agree with him, with HIS position. Consequently, we need to teach students how to choose the side that they can best prove.

Think about state and national assessments, where students are given a set of texts and asked to gather details to write an argument. They are not assessed on their personal opinions — but on what they can prove. We need to teach students not to choose a side based on personal preference, but to find the strongest position based on the texts and the evidence within them.

For this reason I caution teachers against asking students "What do YOU think? What's YOUR opinion? What side are YOU going to write about?" Rather, I would teach them a four-step process to determine the strongest side, and that is to Identify, List, Study, and Decide.

STEP 1: Identifying the different perspectives tends to be hard for a lot of students. They often have SUCH A STRONG personal preference that they don't pause to think that maybe it's possible the other side COULD have some valid points. Consequently, Step 1 is getting students to do some initial reading, just to find out what IS the debate? What are the different opinions? Where is the controversy?

We need to teach writers how to think like someone who believes the other side of the issue. It's about "trying on" that perspective, even if just for a moment.

section_name: Skill 1 — Two-Perspectives Research and Claim Writing
content:
Episode 5 SEC — Skill #1: Two-Perspectives Research, Study, and Claim Writing

During initial research, writers should focus on gathering important facts and details about the issue. This is Step 2. As they read, they should collect specific information for both sides. The goal is to list details that will help decide which side has the strongest argument, the one the writer will eventually support. So, it's important to consider both sides and gather information about them.

It's important to note that in Step 2, students are not compiling a list of REASONS. In fact, don't refer to them as reasons when explaining Step 2. They are only jotting text-based details that they found within the sources. For example: After reading several texts, students collect information FOR and AGAINST genetic engineering. Now, this is just initial research, to get to know the debate. The student will later dive deeper into sources to gather expert quotes and more support, but first he needs to determine WHICH SIDE he is building a case for.

After this initial detail collecting, move onto Step 3. STUDY the lists. Literally, reread the details collected for the different perspectives and consider which side has MORE facts and details? Which one has STRONGER facts and details?

This leads to Step 4 and determining "which is the strongest side?" Ideally, the writer should advocate for THIS position, as it appears to have the more powerful case.

With the strongest side determined, now provide instruction on how to write the claim into a narrowly focused thesis statement. For example: "Genetic engineering of human DNA should not be pursued because it could lead to serious problems and unintended consequences."

Although the standards simply state that we have to teach students to "introduce the claim," we know that includes packaging it within some context. This is when I'd review the SAME strategies we used to write informative introductions. These were described in Episode 3. Before revealing the writer's claim about a topic or text, introduce relevant vocabulary, important people, and/or background knowledge.

section_name: Skill 1 — Writing and Placing the Counterclaim
content:
Episode 5 SEC — Skill #1: Writing and Placing the Counterclaim

Now everything I've addressed so far in essential skill #1 is relevant whether you are teaching students to write a one-sided or a two-sided argument. But for those in grades 7-12, now is when I would provide ADDITIONAL instruction on how to write the counterclaim.

Although the process for writing the counterclaim is similar to writing the claim, make time to show students WHERE to insert it within the introductory paragraph. It typically slides in after the general background information and before the writer's claim. You'll probably also have to teach students how to insert a contrasting transition that connects the two statements:

(counterclaim) "Some people believe that genetic engineering could eradicate diseases and improve the health of individuals of all ages." (claim) "However, despite these possible benefits, there are serious problems and unexpected issues with genetically engineered DNA, so it should not be pursued."

section_name: Skill 2 — Provide Reasons: Generating Original Reasoning
content:
Episode 5 SEC — Skill #2: Provide Reasons

With the claim written, target skill #2: Provide Reasons. Before talking about reasons specifically, start more globally. First tell students that the overall structure of ALL argumentative genres is WHAT and WHY. They ALL begin with the writer's opinion. And then explain it based on reasons. Whether it's a one-sided or two-sided argument, the writer introduces the claim (WHAT he thinks) and moves into the body where he will provide reasons for WHY he thinks it.

Let me caution you not to presume students know HOW to generate reasons. Without direct instruction, many students return to their initial pro-con list to just FIND 3 reasons why.

That would likely play out like this: Imagine a student uses this VERY interesting detail pulled from one of the sources and makes it one of his reasons: "Genetic engineering is dangerous because it could create a double-muscled Belgian blue cow." Huh. If that is a reason, what else will the student be able to say about it? How does a student add supporting details for that?

Don't misunderstand, that cow statement — which comes from the text — is GREAT! And it's a good one to include within the piece. BUT the problem is that students think that THIS is a list of reasons for the writer to choose from. But it's not. In MANY cases it's a list of small facts and specific details.

Reasons are bigger, they're broader. One reason has several small details, examples, or proof to explain it. Consequently, Skill #2 requires teaching students HOW to put together several text details in order to COME UP with their OWN reasons.

section_name: Skill 2 — Original Reasoning vs. Plagiarism and the Table Analogy
content:
Episode 5 SEC — Skill #2: Original Reasoning vs. Plagiarism and the Table Analogy

I emphasize "their OWN reasons" because I recognize that some of what they noted during initial research ARE reasons. Like: "Changing things inside the body might make things worse." That is definitely a broader statement than the blue cow detail. BUT that came from a text; that is another writer's reason. Those are words HE said in a text that the student read. Restating someone else's reason, using his thinking, his ideas as your own — that's plagiarizing. And although state assessments don't typically have rubric criteria for plagiarizing specifically, they do evaluate if the writing has "too much information copied from the original text." The assessment is looking to score the STUDENT'S thinking — it's looking for HIS original reasoning.

Consequently, we have to teach students how to GROUP information that they collected from the sources. To combine some text details in order to generate their OWN reasons and in their OWN words.

That grouping process may look like this: I see "changes might make things worse." So worse to me is it'll create problems. OOH — "could make new genetic problems." OK, so those go together. And a "blue cow" is definitely a problem! But "causes problems" is a little no-duh. It's not much of a reason. Let's see if there are other details I could combine to clarify what I mean by problems. Well these problems happen because "Scientists don't know everything." They don't know "the effects" these changes would have. They only know what they know. They have limited understanding of the potential negative outcomes. Hey, THAT's a reason: "Controlling human genetics may cause negative outcomes because of scientists' limited knowledge." That's MY reason in MY words. None of the authors said "outcome" or "limited knowledge." THAT's ALL ME and my thinking.
skill_title: Original Reasoning vs. Plagiarism and the Table Analogy

section_name: Skill 3 — Support with Evidence: Table Analogy and Counterclaim Development
content:
Episode 5 SEC — Skill #3: Support with Evidence

Let's take a moment to recalibrate: What is it that we want from students when developing reasons within arguments? We ultimately want them to write a paragraph, right? A body paragraph (or more) for EACH reason. We want the reason stated in a topic sentence, and then we want multiple smaller details to support that reason. Specifically we want text evidence and explanations.

This is where the TABLE analogy is a powerful visual. Think of the REASON as the TOP of a table. And OVER it is the claim — it's the table cloth. It's literally above the reason. Each reason is its own table, and we typically need to have 3 reasons to support a claim, so that's like 3 tables pushed together all under the same large table cloth.

Now teach that each table actually has 2 parts, and that brings us to essential Skill #3: Support with Evidence. Looking back at the combined text details that generated a reason, we quickly realize that those SUPPORT the reason, they PROVE the reason. And thus they are the LEGS that hold up that table top. This table analogy helps students understand the difference between reasons-I-think-of and evidence-I-found-in-the-text.

Additionally, this same organizer serves as a pre-write. Each table TOP becomes the TOPic sentence of its own paragraph, with its supporting evidence coming from the text details noted on the corresponding legs.
skill_title: Support with Evidence: Table Analogy and Counterclaim Development

section_name: Counterclaim Integration — Kiddy Table vs. Throughout the Body
content:
Episode 5 SEC — Counterclaim Integration in the Body

For those expected to develop a counterclaim, generate a reason for a fourth time, this one in support of the OPPOSING viewpoint. Go back to the list of text details gathered during the initial research. Combine several details from the WEAKER side of the T-Chart to infer a reason that highlights the merits of the counterclaim. This will add a fourth "table" to the argument — essentially a fourth body paragraph. Think of this like the main adult table during a holiday dinner, and then a smaller kiddy table. This offers a simple way to convert a one-sided argument to a two-sided product. In between the paragraphs SUPPORTING the claim, insert a whole paragraph that acknowledges the opposing view, develops its strongest reason, and then refutes it in a follow up.

While the "kiddy table" approach does incorporate opposing viewpoints and meets the eighth-grade standard, separating the counterclaim into its own paragraph does not demonstrate the sophistication expected at the high school level. Instead of kerplunking the counterclaim in a single section, it should be integrated throughout the body of the writing. Remember, this topic is not black and white; it is complex, controversial, and multi-faceted. Therefore, it's important to acknowledge that none of the three reasons and their supporting evidence are perfect; each one has its own flaws, weaknesses, and limitations.

So teach students how to incorporate individual sentences that acknowledge weaknesses throughout the body paragraph. To do this, revisit the tables-and-legs organizer. Reread each reason AND its supporting evidence from the perspective of someone who disagrees with the position. Think about the information as someone who may not share the same beliefs, values, or knowledge. Consider what objections this reader might raise in response to each reason you generated and piece of evidence you plan to provide. Record these objections as additional legs under the same table top. And if you mark these legs with an X, you can easily remind yourself that you have planned to include some limitations.

Then, when composing the paragraph, make sure to address these weaknesses and refute them effectively.
skill_title: Kiddy Table vs. Throughout the Body

section_name: Skill 4 — Conclude the Argument and Key Takeaways
content:
Episode 5 SEC — Skill #4: Conclude the Argument and Key Takeaways

Concluding the argument is the 4th essential skill. Conclusions are most effective when they are short and impactful. But this can be a challenge to achieve when having to reiterate the claim and the counterclaim. Therefore, show students how to restate both within the conclusion using tighter, more succinct sentences than they originally used within the introduction. Since the entire piece focused on this debate, a lengthy repetition is unnecessary. Similarly, summarizing all the reasons isn't essential — or required in the conclusion — either.

Instead, students should focus on what's at stake if the reader ignores the writer's claim and accepts the opposing viewpoint. This "what's at stake" approach leaves the reader remembering why the issue is so important and why the writer's position is the stronger one.

As I wrap up this video, let me identify TWO important takeaways.

FIRST: Persuasive-writing skills lay the foundation for argumentative skills. Consequently, regardless of your grade level, consider teaching students how to construct a one-sided argument before introducing the complexities of the counterclaim. Teach all four essential skills within a brief introductory unit, then spiral through them again, adding the counterclaim expectations within future units.

A second important takeaway is about that list of text details that was originally created, back in essential skill #1. That list-making process impacts 3 of the 4 most essential argumentative skills. (SKILL 1) The initial list of details helps the writer identify the strongest side and write his claim. (SKILL 2) The same list provides the details to combine in order to generate reasons in support of the claim. (SKILL 3) And the text details collected and grouped also become the evidence needed for developing each of those different reasons.

This 4-step process for determining the strongest side has benefits far beyond helping students get started. And thus, it's a powerful component to any argumentative writing unit. I encourage you to review your state standards and make adjustments in order to prioritize these 4 standards-based skills. By targeting these essential skills when teaching argumentative writing, we take the next step toward building better writers.
skill_title: Conclude the Argument and Key Takeaways
